title: 'It Was a Tricky Wicket': Santner Reflects as India Edge Wellington ODI
excerpt: New Zealand's captain praised both bowling attacks after a low-scoring second ODI in Wellington, where India won by four runs under DLS to lead the series 2-0.
body:
• India beat New Zealand by four runs under the DLS method in the second ODI in Wellington, after rain ended play with India 113 for 7 in 26 overs, four runs ahead of the par score.
  • New Zealand were bowled out for 134 in 41 overs, with Gurnoor Brar taking 4 for 30 and Daryl Mitchell's 55 the only half-century of the match.
  • Captain Mitchell Santner called the surface "a tricky wicket," praised both bowling attacks, and admitted New Zealand were "a little bit under" a competitive total, saying 160-180 was reachable.
  • India lead the series 2-0; the third ODI is in Hamilton on Tuesday, November 10. Blair Tickner, replaced under concussion protocols, is back at the team hotel.

India beat New Zealand by four runs under the DLS method in the second ODI at Hnry Stadium in Wellington on Saturday, taking a 2-0 lead in the five-match series — and afterwards, captain Mitchell Santner had a simple explanation for a match in which no batting side looked comfortable: the pitch. New Zealand were bowled out for 134 in 41 overs, and India were 113 for 7 after 26 overs, four runs ahead of the DLS par score, when rain ended the contest, according to ANI reporting carried by NewKerala.

"It was a tricky wicket. There is no hiding it. I think they bowled really well, especially at the top, challenged us, and obviously, wickets at the start are never ideal."

— Mitchell Santner, New Zealand captain

Bowlers on top from the start

India elected to bowl first and their seamers exploited the moisture. Auqib Nabi dismissed both openers and Anshul Kamboj removed Henry Nicholls to leave New Zealand 23 for 3, before Gurnoor Brar broke the innings open, dismissing Tom Latham and Glenn Phillips in the same over and later Santner himself to finish with career-best figures of 4 for 30. Daryl Mitchell held the innings together with 55 off 104 balls, sharing a half-century stand with Santner (31 off 38), but 134 never looked enough — even on this surface.

Santner, however, refused to hide entirely behind the pitch. "I think we were still probably a little bit under at the halfway stage, knowing that there was still a little bit in it," he said, in comments also carried by IANS via Asia Post. "As a batting unit, we know it was going to be a tricky surface. But even if there was a potential way of scraping to 160 or 180, we could have gone from there."

India's chase nearly slipped away

Chasing 135, India were reduced to 47 for 4, with Shubman Gill and Virat Kohli falling cheaply to Jacob Duffy. Shreyas Iyer made 30 and KL Rahul an unbeaten 26, but Kyle Jamieson took 3 for 35 and Duffy struck again to reduce India to 113 for 7, with the match in the balance when the rain arrived. Santner praised his own attack for refusing to let a small target become a formality: "Like we said at Eden Park, it would have been easy for us to just go out there and expect things to happen. But we bowled really well. We started well, and the only way to get into that target was to take wickets at the top."

Santner did not bowl himself: "It was one of those wickets where the seamers looked pretty challenging on. I know Axar bowled quite nicely, but the Indian quicks were in and around it as well, and they all bowled pretty well." On Blair Tickner, replaced by concussion substitute Matthew Fisher after a blow to the helmet while batting, he said: "He is back at the hotel, so hopefully he pulls up okay. But he has had a concussion recently, so it is one of those ones you want to give it some time."

What it means

India's 2-0 lead means New Zealand must win in Hamilton on Tuesday, November 10 to keep the series alive. Santner's assessment frames the task: his bowlers showed that early wickets can drag any chase into trouble, but his batters must post a defendable total even on surfaces offering the seamers this much help.
